```{r child = "helpers/_setup.Rmd"}
```

```{r}
#| label: library
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
library(housepi)
housepi_theme_set()
set.seed(42)
```

We provide a simple model to generate synthetic household datasets.
Let's assume that each individual can be represented with a single variable $\theta$, encoding for the provided covariates.
We declare the covariates of interest when we generate a new sampler calling `new_household_sampler`.

```{r}
# define individual features from dataset covariates assumed not independent
hhsampler <- new_household_sampler(
  # categorical data: levels to be considered
  sex = list(levels = c("M", "F")),
  # numerical data to be factorized: breaks for binning
  age = list(breaks = c(0, 15, 25, 50))
)

# internal encoding and associated hierarchy
hhsampler$hierarchy
```

The order of the definition is important, setting a "hierarchy" across covariates (this will be used for the modelling, see next section).
Here sex `"F"` has priority on `"M"`, and ages `[25, 50)` have priority on ages `[0,15)`.
Also, encoding implies an implicit representation of a dataset, e.g.

```{r}
# example house dataset
eg_house <- data.frame(house_id = "HH_1",
                       age = c(43, 39, 12, 7),
                       sex = c("M", "F", "F", "M"))

# underlying representation of data
hhsampler$decode(hhsampler$encode(eg_house))
```

We now define a model able to extract distributions of such features within a household, with the final goal to sample from it.

# Hierarchical model definition

In order to capture at the same time covariate marginals and a realistic generational-based structure within household,
we propose the following assumptions on the structure of households.

For a household with a single individual (size $n=1$) with encoding $\theta$, the model assigns a probability:

$$
P[\lbrace\theta\rbrace] =
P(\theta\vert{n=1})
$$

For larger households ($n\geq{2}$), we assume a hierarchical structure as follows:

* two household members $\theta_{1}$, $\theta_{2}$ are considered "principal" according to the hierarchy of the features;
* size $n$ is considered conditioned on the encodings of principal members;
* all other members $\theta_{3},\;\dots,\;\theta_{n}$ are conditioned on principal members.

The probability factorizes to:

$$
P[\lbrace\theta_{1},\dots,{\theta}_{n}\rbrace] =
P({\theta_{1}},{\theta_{2}})
P(n\vert {\theta_{1}},{\theta_{2}})
\prod_{k=2}^{n} P({\theta_{k}}\vert{\theta_{1}},{\theta_{2}})
$$

For a generic household in our dataset, the probability reads

$$
p_{1} P[\lbrace\theta\rbrace]
+
(1 - p_{1}) P[\lbrace\theta_{1},\dots,{\theta}_{n}\rbrace]
$$

where $p_1$ is the probability of finding a household with a single member in our dataset.

# Compute marginals and generate datasets

```{r}
hhsampler |>
  # compute marginal distributions
  compute_household_marginals(housepi::sarscov2_2021_icofs) |>
  # sample 5 households
  sample_households(5)
```
